newsitem.title: TURKEY: Cracks in Turkey coalition after army warning.
newsitem.headline: Cracks in Turkey coalition after army warning.

text.p: Cracks appeared in Turkey's ruling coalition on Tuesday after the country's generals demanded an end to Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's Islamist fervour.
Partner Tansu Ciller was quoted as saying she would pull out of the alliance if Erbakan did not try to stamp out Islamist activism soon.
"We are not locked into the government. We will pull out if the conditions require it," the Milliyet newspaper quoted conservative Ciller as telling her True Path Party aides on Monday.
Istanbul stocks plummeted 7.62 percent in early trading on Tuesday on political worries and inflation figures that were worse than expected, brokers said.
The military-dominated National Security Council (NSC) warned Erbakan at the weekend to reverse recent Islamist zeal partly encouraged by his Welfare Party.
Health Minister Yildirim Aktuna, a member of Ciller's wing, predicted Erbakan could quit rather than disappoint his Islamist backers by heeding the army.
"If Erbakan does not feel the need to carry out the decisions of the NSC, he may resign," Milliyet quoted Aktuna as saying.
The Hurriyet newspaper said other members of the pro-Western True Path wanted to split the eight-month-old coalition now.
Despite the friction, there was no immediate sign that Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, would lose two parliamentary challenges later on Tuesday.
MPs are to gather at 1500 (1300 GMT) to vote on whether to go ahead with an opposition censure motion against the coalition within a week.
Deputies will also vote on opening an inquiry into Justice Minister Sevket Kazan, an Islamist and close aide of Erbakan. Defeat on either issue would be a major blow to the government.
Kazan has been at the centre of a row over Welfare's alleged backing of Islamist militants.
Kazan is accused of abusing his position by visiting a Welfare mayor jailed for organising an Islamist protest in the Ankara district of Sincan also attended by Iran's ambassador.
The army sent tanks onto the streets of Sincan in a thinly-veiled warning to Welfare.
Erbakan has brushed off the generals' latest warning.
"In Turkey governments are formed in parliament, not in the National Security Council. Laws are made in parliament," he said.
Political analysts say he ignores the generals at his peril.
The army, which frequently leads opinion polls as the country's most respected institution, has ousted three governments since 1960.
It has a free hand in the fight against Kurdish rebels in the mountainous southeast and plays a major role in Turkey's many disputes with neighbours Greece and Cyprus.
Young officers are taught to idolise Turkey's secularist founder Kemal Ataturk, himself a military man.
